parts: Lesson 19: Mental Health and Hygiene — Summary
Concepts of mental health and hygiene

Health is a state of physical, mental, social and spiritual well-being. Mental health is one component: an optimum level of emotional and behavioural adjustment, a state of harmony between the needs, desires, aspirations and attitudes of the individual and the conditions of the external environment. Hygiene means keeping oneself and one's living and working areas neat and clean to prevent illness; mental hygiene extends this to the art of developing, maintaining and promoting behavioural, emotional and social skills to sustain good mental health. Strategies of mental hygiene: (A) Reality contact – a realistic appraisal of one's own reactions, emotions and abilities avoids disappointment; (B) Impulse control – control over impulsive behaviour; (C) Self-esteem – self-concept is the sum total of what a person is aware of about the self (statements about 'I' or 'me'); self-esteem is its evaluative component, and a sense of personal adequacy is essential for mental health; (D) Positive thoughts – negative thoughts create anger, hate, jealousy, fear, despair and harm the endocrine system, while positive thinking creates love, joy, hope, compassion, empathy and optimism and strengthens coping.
Mental health, mental ill-health and mental illness

Mental ill-health is the absence of the qualities of positive mental health (e.g. frequent negative feelings and attitudes about others). Mental illness is a broad term for disorders of behaviour caused by faulty perception, emotion, thinking and attitude, leading to problems of adjustment in society.

Haphazard daily routine, short-tempered and irritating behaviour, anger and aggression, restlessness, increased or poor appetite and indigestion, irregular sleep (insomnia, disturbed sleep, narcolepsy), poor interpersonal relationships, anxiety and worry, negative attitude toward self and others, withdrawal, abnormal physiological conditions (blood pressure, palpitation, pulse), excessive use of drugs (alcohol, tranquillizers, hallucinogens), smoking and tobacco use. If these occur often or for long, mental disorders may develop.

Four aspects: Ahara (right food), Vihara (right recreation), Achara (right routine) and Vichara (right thinking). Food: fresh fruits and vegetables with fibre, green vegetables, beans, honey, curd, milk, balanced proportions, fixed meal times, chewing well; vegetarian food is safe and invigorating. Routine: Ritucharya (food and activity according to the seasons: light, fluid food in summer; sweet and salty milk products and ghee in winter and autumn; light food with less oil in spring; astringent, acidic, salty and sweet tastes in the rainy season), Dincharya (day routine) and Ratricharya (night routine): get up before sunrise, drink water first, excretion, cleaning teeth, massage and bath, with proper time for each activity. Recreation: exercise and morning walks make the body light and strong, increase immunity, excrete toxins through perspiration, control heart disease and diabetes, delay ageing and purify blood; music helps. Thinking: a mentally healthy person has self-satisfaction, an accommodative intellect, ability to accept criticism, understanding of others' emotional needs and self-control, free from greed, fear, anger, jealousy, guilt or worry.

We fail to organise activities in the 24 hours, causing pressure and frustration. An activity schedule is a structured routine with activities listed and sequenced by importance (study, play and sleep); a diary also helps. Principles: (I) prepare a list of work (a day in advance at night); (II) prioritise: the toughest task first, the easiest when tired; (III) identify uninterrupted periods for tasks needing sustained attention; (IV) keep a flexible schedule for unexpected events; (V) set aside time for exercise and yoga; (VI) plan leisure activity (music, gardening, painting, sports) for rest and break.
